# Something Completely Different

- Everything this term had **one** response variable
  - t-test: one measurement, two groups
  - regression: one measurement against one other
  - ANOVA: one measurement across several groups
- Today: **six measurements at once**, and no groups to compare
  - not *"is A different from B?"*
  - but *"what is the **shape** of this whole dataset?"* 🔴

# Today Has No p-Values

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- PCA is **not a test**
  - no null hypothesis
  - no p-value
  - no assumptions to check
  - nothing passes or fails
- It is a way of **looking** at data that has too many columns to plot
- The question is never *"is it significant?"*
  - it is always **"does this make sense?"**
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-important
**⚠️ Set down one habit**

For nine weeks, "did it work?" meant "is p small?"

Today you judge your result by whether you can **explain what the axes mean**.
:::
::::
::::::

# Goals for Today

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- **See** the data in 3-D — and why six columns cannot be drawn
- Notice that the columns are **correlated**
- See **where a principal component comes from**
- Know why you must **scale** first
- Run it: `prcomp()`
- Read **variance explained**, draw a **scree plot**
- **Check** PC1 against Pokémon you already know
- **Hover** over the new picture to find them
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
**Tools today:**

- `tidyverse`
- `plotly` — you installed it for the mapping weeks

**Data:** 🔴 **all 1,025 Pokémon**, six battle stats each

::: callout-tip
**No new packages.** `prcomp()` is built into R.
:::
::::
::::::

# Why Pokémon

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- Because you can **check the answer**
  - PCA hands back new axes that it **invented**
  - you have to decide whether they mean anything
  - that is nearly impossible on data you do not know
- If an axis puts **Magikarp** at one end and **Mewtwo** at the other, you know *exactly* what it found
- 1,025 is plenty of data — and **hovering** tells you who any dot is
- Same method as gene expression, soil chemistry, skull measurements
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 The six stats**

- `hp` — hit points
- `attack` — physical attack
- `defense` — physical defence
- `sp_attack` — special attack
- `sp_defense` — special defence
- `speed` — speed

Game-design numbers, but they behave exactly like six measurements off an animal.
:::
::::
::::::

# 🧩 Chunk 1 of 4 · Look at the Data First

**We will cover:**

- reading the data and marking the legendaries
- three stats in 3-D — and why six is impossible

# Read It In

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r read-pokemon}
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)

pokemon <- read_csv("data/pokemon_1025.csv") %>%
  mutate(status = case_when(
    is_legendary ~ "legendary",
    is_mythical  ~ "mythical",
    TRUE         ~ "regular"))

pokemon %>% count(status)
```
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
- 1,025 rows — one per Pokémon
- `status` is **one** column built from two TRUE/FALSE ones
  - first matching line wins
  - `TRUE ~` catches everything left over
- We will **colour** by `status` — PCA never sees it

::: callout-note
**🧠 Mythical?**

A second "rare and special" group in the game — Mew is mythical, Mewtwo is legendary.
:::
::::
::::::

# Three Stats, in 3-D

```{r plot-3d}
#| eval: !expr is_html
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.6
plot_ly(pokemon, x = ~attack, y = ~defense, z = ~speed,
        color = ~status, text = ~name,
        colors = c("firebrick", "darkorange", "grey60"),
        type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers", marker = list(size = 3))
```

```{r plot-3d-static}
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr '!is_html'
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
ggplot(pokemon, aes(attack, defense, color = status)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("firebrick", "darkorange", "grey60")) +
  labs(caption = "Static view - the HTML slides have a 3-D plot you can rotate")
```

# What That Plot Shows

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- **Drag to rotate it** — every dot is one Pokémon
  - from some angles: a shapeless blob
  - from others: a long, spread-out cloud
  - same data, **different amount you can see**
- **Hover** — the name pops up
  - red / orange (legendary, mythical) sit out at the **big** end
- But this is only **3 of the 6 stats**
  - `hp`, `sp_attack`, `sp_defense` are missing
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-important
**✅ Hold on to this**

Rotating to find the angle that shows the **most spread** is exactly what PCA does.

It just does it in **six** dimensions, where we cannot rotate anything by hand.
:::
::::
::::::

# Six Columns Is Too Many to Plot

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- One measurement → a histogram
- Two → a scatterplot
- Three → the 3-D plot you just spun
- **Six → nothing**
  - there is no six-dimensional plot, and never will be
- All the pairs instead? **15 scatterplots**
  - nobody can hold 15 plots in their head
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ The real problem**

**"Which Pokémon are similar to each other?"** is a question about all six numbers **at the same time**.

Looking at them two at a time cannot answer it.
:::
::::
::::::

# Make Them a Table of Their Own

```{r stats-table}
poke_stats <- pokemon %>%
  select(hp, attack, defense, sp_attack, sp_defense, speed)

dim(poke_stats)
```

::: callout-note
**🧠 Why a separate table**

- PCA needs **numbers only** — no names, no types, no `status`
- The rows stay in the **same order** as `pokemon`
  - that is what lets us glue the results back on later
  - **never sort one and not the other**
:::

# 🧩 Chunk 2 of 4 · Where the New Axes Come From

**We will cover:**

- the correlation table — the raw material
- why you do **not** drop correlated columns
- PC1 drawn with just two stats, then the shadow analogy

# Do the Stats Move Together?

```{r correlation}
poke_stats %>%
  cor() %>%
  round(2)
```

# Reading That Matrix

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- The diagonal is all `1.00` — each column against itself. Ignore it
- The strongest pairs:
  - `defense` & `sp_defense`: **0.50**
  - `sp_attack` & `sp_defense`: **0.49**
  - `hp` & `attack`: **0.48**
  - `attack` & `defense`: **0.47**
- And one that is nothing at all:
  - `speed` & `defense`: **0.01**
- So six columns are **not** six independent facts
  - they **overlap** — knowing one tells you something about another
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-important
**✅ This is what makes PCA work**

**Correlation is redundancy.**

PCA's whole job is to squeeze the redundancy out.

If all six were completely unrelated, there would be nothing to squeeze — six axes in, six equally useless axes out.
:::
::::
::::::

# "Shouldn't I Drop the Correlated Ones?"

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- **No.** That rule is from **regression**
  - there, two correlated predictors fight over one slope
- In PCA, correlation is the **fuel**, not a problem
  - correlated stats simply **land on the same axis**
  - that is the redundancy being squeezed out
- PCA is **built from this correlation table**
  - with `scale. = TRUE`, that table is literally the input
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ The one real caution**

Do not put in the **same thing twice**.

A "total stats" column next to the six stats it was added up from would count everything twice.

Here the biggest correlation is **0.50** — nowhere near a duplicate.
:::
::::
::::::

# Where PC1 Comes From — With Two Stats

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r two-stat-demo}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4.2
two_df <- pokemon %>%
  transmute(attack  = as.numeric(scale(attack)),
            defense = as.numeric(scale(defense)))

ggplot(two_df, aes(attack, defense)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, color = "grey40") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
              color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_abline(slope = -1, intercept = 0,
              color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.3, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 3.2, y = 3.7, label = "PC1",
           color = "firebrick", fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = -2.6, y = 3.4, label = "PC2",
           color = "steelblue", fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-3, 4), ylim = c(-3, 4)) +
  labs(x = "attack (scaled)", y = "defense (scaled)")
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
- `attack` vs `defense`, r = 0.47
  - the cloud is **stretched along a diagonal**
- **PC1** (red) = the line along the **longest** stretch
  - it holds **73%** of the spread in these two stats
- **PC2** (blue) = **right angles** to PC1
  - it holds the leftover 27%
- Strong correlation → long, thin cloud → PC1 holds a lot
:::
:::::

# The Same Idea, in Six Dimensions

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- Your data is a cloud of 1,025 points in **6-D** space
- **PC1** = the direction through that cloud with the **most spread**
- **PC2** = the most spread that is **left**, at right angles to PC1
- **PC3** = the next leftover, and so on
- Six columns in → six PCs out, in **order of usefulness**
- Each PC is a **blend** of the old columns:

$$\text{PC1} = a_1\,\text{hp} + a_2\,\text{attack} + \ldots$$
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-note
**🧠 Two words you need**

**Loading** — how much an original stat contributes to a PC. *What the axis is made of* — the $a$'s.

**Score** — where one Pokémon sits along that PC. *Its new measurement.*

Loadings describe the **axis**. Scores describe the **Pokémon**.
:::
::::
::::::

# The Shadow Analogy 🔦

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- Hold your hand in front of a lamp
  - your hand is **3-D**, the shadow is **2-D**
  - you lost a dimension — but it still looks like a hand
- **Rotate** your hand
  - some angles: you recognise it instantly
  - others: a shapeless blob
- **Same hand. Same wall. Different amount kept**
- That is the 3-D plot you spun — now in six dimensions
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-tip
**🎯 That is PCA**

PCA finds the angle that casts the **most informative shadow** of the 6-D cloud — the one where the points stay as spread out as possible.

Then it reports what that shadow is made of.
:::
::::
::::::

# First: You Must Scale

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r scale-why}
poke_stats %>%
  summarise(across(everything(),
                   ~ sd(.x)))
```

- PCA chases **spread**
  - unscaled, the column with the **biggest numbers** wins by default
- Pokémon stats happen to be on similar scales (sd 27–30)
  - real data almost never is
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ A worked disaster**

Measure animals in **grams** and **kilometres**.

- body mass in grams: thousands
- home range in km: maybe 0.4

Unscaled, PC1 would be **entirely mass** — it would only tell you which unit you typed.
:::
::::
::::::

# Scaling, In One Argument

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- `scale. = TRUE` turns every column into **standard deviations from its own mean**
- After scaling, every column has
  - mean **0**
  - standard deviation **1**
- All six compete **fairly**, and the units cancel out
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-important
**⚠️ Mind the full stop**

The argument is **`scale.`** — with a dot:

``` r
prcomp(poke_stats, scale. = TRUE)
```

`scale` was already an R function. Leave the dot off and you get an error.

**Almost always use `scale. = TRUE`.**
:::
::::
::::::

# 🧩 Chunk 3 of 4 · Run It and Read It

**We will cover:** `prcomp()`, `summary()`, variance explained, and the scree plot.

# One Line

```{r run-pca}
poke_pca <- prcomp(poke_stats, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
```

::: callout-note
**🧠 That is the entire analysis**

- `center = TRUE` — subtract each column's mean
- `scale. = TRUE` — divide by each column's standard deviation
- Nothing prints — the result is stored in `poke_pca`
- Everything from here on is **reading the result** — the part that takes judgement
:::

# What Came Back

```{r pca-summary}
summary(poke_pca)
```

# Reading `summary()`

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- Ignore the first row (`Standard deviation`)
- **`Proportion of Variance`** — share of the total spread each PC holds
  - **PC1: 44.1%**
  - **PC2: 18.4%**
  - PC3: 14.7%
- **`Cumulative Proportion`** — the running total
  - PC1 alone: **44.1%**
  - PC1 + PC2: **62.5%**
  - all six: 100%, always
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-important
**✅ The headline**

**Two** invented axes carry **62.5%** of everything in six columns.

So one flat scatterplot of PC1 against PC2 shows you nearly **two-thirds** of the whole dataset.
:::
::::
::::::

# "Variance Explained", In Plain Words

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- **Variance** = how spread out things are
- Total variance = every way these 1,025 Pokémon differ, across all six stats
- PC1 holds 44.1% of that
  - throw away all six stats
  - keep **only** each Pokémon's PC1 score
  - you still have **44%** of how they differ
- **One number instead of six**, for 44% of the picture
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Not 44% of the Pokémon**

And not 44% accuracy.

It is 44% of the **total variation** — of the differences between them.
:::
::::
::::::

# How Much Variance Per Axis

```{r var-table}
var_df <- tibble(
  PC      = paste0("PC", 1:6),
  percent = round(100 * poke_pca$sdev^2 / sum(poke_pca$sdev^2), 1)
)

var_df
```

::: callout-note
**🧠 Where that came from**

- `poke_pca$sdev` = each PC's standard deviation
- square it → variance; ÷ total → a share; × 100 → a percent
- Same numbers `summary()` printed — but in a **data frame**, so we can plot them
:::

# The Scree Plot

```{r scree}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(var_df, aes(x = PC, y = percent)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent), vjust = -0.4)
```

# Reading a Scree Plot

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- **Scree** = the rubble at the foot of a cliff — the shape the bars make
- Look for the **elbow**: where the bars stop dropping steeply
- Here:
  - PC1 stands **way** above the rest
  - PC2 onwards step down gently
- **Keep two**: the big one, plus the one we will learn to name
  - and know you are holding 62.5%
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ There is no rule**

People argue about the elbow constantly. Rough guides:

- keep PCs until the cumulative total passes \~70–80%
- keep the ones **before** the flat part
- keep the ones you can **interpret**

That last one is the most useful.
:::
::::
::::::

# 🧩 Chunk 4 of 4 · Does PC1 Mean Anything?

**We will cover:**

- what PC1 is made of
- who sits at each end of it
- the picture, with names on hover

# What PC1 Is Made Of

```{r loadings-peek}
round(poke_pca$rotation[, 1:2], 2)
```

::: callout-important
**✅ Look at the PC1 column: every number is positive (0.31 to 0.44)**

- A Pokémon scores high on PC1 by being high on **all six stats at once**
- PC1 is an **"overall power"** axis
- PC2 has **minus signs** — it is doing something different. Next class
:::

# Where Does Each Pokémon Sit?

```{r scores}
poke_scores <- pokemon %>%
  mutate(PC1 = poke_pca$x[, 1],
         PC2 = poke_pca$x[, 2])

poke_scores %>%
  select(name, hp, attack, speed, PC1, PC2) %>%
  head(3)
```

::: callout-note
**🧠 `poke_pca$x` holds the scores**

- one row per Pokémon, one column per PC, **same row order** as the data
- that is why `mutate()` can glue them straight on
- scores are in **standard deviations**: 0 = average, negative = below average
:::

# The Top of PC1

```{r top-pc1}
poke_scores %>%
  arrange(desc(PC1)) %>%
  select(name, status, PC1) %>%
  head(6)
```

# The Bottom of PC1

```{r bottom-pc1}
poke_scores %>%
  arrange(PC1) %>%
  select(name, status, PC1) %>%
  head(6)
```

# That Is the Validation 🎣

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- **Top of PC1:** Arceus, Ho-Oh, Giratina, Lunala, Eternatus, Reshiram
  - **every one a legendary or mythical**
- **Bottom of PC1:** Wishiwashi, Blipbug, Sunkern, **Magikarp**, Snom, Weedle
  - the famously useless ones
- Nobody told PCA which Pokémon were strong
  - there is **no "power" column** in the file
  - it sorted them by overall strength **on its own**
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-important
**✅ Why this matters beyond Pokémon**

This is the check you run on **every** PCA.

You cannot test whether an axis is "real". But you *can* look at what sits at each end and ask whether it lines up with something you already know.

If it does not, be very careful.
:::
::::
::::::

# Put a Number on It

```{r legendary-mean}
poke_scores %>%
  group_by(status) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_PC1 = round(mean(PC1), 2))
```

::: callout-note
**🧠 Reading it**

- 71 legendaries average **PC1 = 2.38**; 23 mythicals **2.25**; the other 931 **−0.24**
- Scores are in standard deviations → the rare ones sit about **2.5 sd above** the crowd
- On an axis built **without ever being told** they existed
:::

# The Picture — Hover Over It

```{r pca-plotly}
#| eval: !expr is_html
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.3
pca_plot <- ggplot(poke_scores,
                   aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = status, text = name)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6)

ggplotly(pca_plot, tooltip = "text")
```

```{r pca-plotly-static}
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr '!is_html'
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
ggplot(poke_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = status)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(caption = "Static view - in the HTML slides you can hover for names")
```

# Reading That Picture

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
- Every dot is one Pokémon, on **two invented axes**
  - **left ↔ right** = weak ↔ strong *(PC1, 44.1%)*
  - **up ↔ down** = something else *(PC2, 18.4%)*
- Legendaries and mythicals pile up on the **right**
- **Hover** to check:
  - Magikarp on the far left
  - Mewtwo on the far right
  - who is that one **way** up at the top?
- `text = name` is not a real ggplot aesthetic — `ggplotly()` picks it up for the hover
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-tip
**🎯 Close dots = similar Pokémon**

Two dots near each other have **similar stat profiles overall** — the all-six-at-once question we could not answer with 15 scatterplots.

And this one plot holds **62.5%** of the six columns.
:::
::::
::::::

# What We Have, and What Is Missing

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
**We have:**

- two axes holding 62.5% of six columns
- PC1 = **"overall power"**, checked against Magikarp and the legendaries
- a picture you can hover over

**We do not have:**

- any idea what **PC2** means
- a way to see the six original stats **on** the picture

Both are next class.
:::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-tip
**🎯 A hint about PC2**

In PC2, `defense` is **+0.58** and `speed` is **−0.70**.

A big positive and a big negative on the same axis means a **trade-off**, not a total.

Which trade-off? Next class.
:::
::::
::::::

# Recap

- PCA is **not a test** — no p-value, nothing to reject
- Six columns **cannot be plotted**; three in 3-D already need rotating
- PCA works **because** the columns are correlated — **do not drop** them
- **PC1** = the direction of most spread; **PC2** = most of what is left, at right angles
- Think **shadows**: the most informative angle on a cloud you cannot see
- **Always `scale. = TRUE`**
- **PC1 = 44.1%, PC2 = 18.4%, together 62.5%**
- The **scree plot** shows where to stop — judgement, not a rule
- **Validate by looking at the ends** — Magikarp at one end, the legendaries at the other ✅

::: callout-note
**✅ Next**

Open the activity and type it in. Next class: what PC2 means, and the biplot. 🔴
:::
